- It has been typical during recent metals industry gatherings to see prices move decisively up or down under the common thread of increasing optimism/pessimism over the week of the meeting itself.  But this time, at CESCO in Santiago during the first week of the month, copper participants clearly fell into two fairly equal camps of bulls and bears and, consequently, this was reflected in the direction – or, rather, a lack of it – of copper prices on the LME. 

- March data releases from China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) reveal some superficial contradictions which can only be explained by stock changes of intermediate copper semis.  The weak semis production figures when set against the context of strong end-use output has to imply that de-stocking has been responsible for the apparent poor performance from the semis producers.  Provided that end-use output remains robust, the pipeline between cathode consumers, semis manufacturers and end-users will need to be replenished. 

- Wedding fever is in the air in the UK ahead of the Royal nuptials at the end of April and as with every such occasion, the groom will be nervously waiting and hoping that the bride does indeed turn up.  With global demand expectations now so closely wedded to the Chinese market given its relative size it was always going to be its performance that determined the global outturn this year.  However, after making her first tentative steps in March, Chinese consumption is beginning to head down the aisle, with the groom, a market deficit, waiting gleefully at the altar. 

- Spot TC/RCs (miners to traders) have moved a little lower after starting the month at $115/t & 11.5c/lb and then easing back towards $110/t & 11c/lb for prompt clean material.  With spot rates at their highest levels for more than 5 years and with a narrowing of the SFHE:LME arbitrage towards parity, it is perhaps a little surprising that Chinese buying hasn’t picked up materially, particularly with Q1 concentrate imports trailing last year’s levels by almost 17%. Some traders believe that Chinese smelting companies are pricing themselves out of the market with unrealistic expectations.  While we hear that spot business has been concluded in China at $125/t & 12.5c/lb of late, traders are extremely reluctant to entertain numbers above this level.

## Market Developments 

**Copper prices lack direction during CESCO…** It has been typical during recent metals industry gatherings to see prices move decisively up or down under the common thread of increasing optimism/pessimism over the week of the meeting itself.  But this time, at CESCO in Santiago during the first week of the month, copper participants clearly fell into two fairly equal camps of bulls and bears and, consequently, this was reflected in the direction – or, rather, a lack of it – of copper prices on the LME.  With the bears citing China’s less than convincing performance thus far this year, sufficient overhang of metal stocks and high prices eroding the metal’s attractiveness among consumers now eager to try alternatives, copper fell to its month’s low of US$9251/t ($4.20/lb) on the 5<sup>th</sup> .  The bulls countered with a need for patience to see China come back into the market and a lack of new projects on the 2012-2013 horizon, and cash quotes on the LME picked up $225/t the very next day. 

**..but spurred on briefly by encouraging March Chinese trade data** After all was said and done this year at CESCO, it was quickly forgotten by the final day of that week when Chinese authorities released headline trade data for March, which was sufficiently optimistic to add a further $125/t to LME quotes on Friday 8<sup>th</sup> and bring cash to US$9823/t ($4.46/lb).  In theory, then, the bulls at CESCO will probably have embarked on their journeys home feeling justified about their view.  But as this price will no doubt turn out to be the month’s high, the bears could also go home feeling somewhat justified in holding their jaded near-term outlook.  The fact that the market cannot talk itself past the US$9900/t level (c.$4.50/lb) indeed suggests that it is being held back by the twin pressures of concern over Chinese metal stocks and poor offtake.  The metal lost US$500/t over the course of the next five days and, aside from one day of minicorrection, it has largely traded at that US$9350/t level ($4.25/lb) for the second half of the month.  With the LME also being closed for three bank holidays in April (and for one more in the first week of May), perhaps this too is contributing to the general air of ennui over copper markets and, indeed, over the rest of the metals complex. 

**Little news of mine supply disruption during the month…** Generally, concerns over burgeoning Chinese bonded warehouse stocks more than overshadowed news about supply disruptions.  Also, when there was – for example, Rio Tinto’s noted downgrade of its forecast attributable copper output this year from 562kt to 539kt – there was frequently a countering news item to calm any market fears.  In this instance, a new labour contract was accepted by three trade unions at

Codelco’s El Teniente division, promising to keep that operation steady through to the end of October, 2014. Codelco had offered a pay rise of 3.85% plus bonuses and soft loans worth c.US$32k. In fact, many first quarter production reports indicated either higher copper for the quarter just gone or the quarter underway, and offset other reports (Anglo American, First Quantum, QuadraFNX, Rio Tinto, for example) indicating output shortfalls. **..and China’s latest attempts to reduce speculative buying also bearish for copper** Meanwhile, right at the end of March, the Chinese government published a new set of rules which were designed to quell the country’s use of copper as an investment vehicle for property speculators. The new rules came into effect on April 1st , but there was little immediate clarity behind them or agreement amongst market players on what they meant for copper prices going forward. In summary, the new rules are another element to the government’s efforts to tighten credit, and while this may translate into lower copper imports in April (i.e. a bearish short-term influence), it should have the effect of reducing the amount of metal that is purportedly going into bonded warehouses merely for investment purposes, rather than for firstuse consumption. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

**Stronger dollar, fresh tremors in Japan, also dampen copper price strength…** Factors outside the immediacy of metals also tempered any price gain. The US dollar, which had been weakening for the first half of the month, then firmed up (mildly). And then Japan endured a series of aftershocks to its devastating March earthquake and tsunami, which dented investor confidence in the country’s ability to re-build. Both conditions suppressed metals prices. Then, casting a wider eye brought investors to question how strong could Chinese _April_ trade data possibly be if March’s refined copper production

figure was up by 22.7% on February and by 10.3% for Q1 on Q1 2010.  Presumably the intent with this unanswerable question was indeed to quell interest in seeing higher prices, and it worked in a market that remains clearly unnerved by the slightest indicator either side of the line. 

**...as does Chinese monetary policy** Ultimately, whether it is issues over physical metal demand and metal stockpiling or monetary policy, copper’s price direction always seems to be guided by news from China.  Just as the rate of decline in copper prices was slowing on the 13<sup>th</sup> , there was renewed debate that Chinese authorities would increase the bank reserve lending ratio a fourth time this year by 0.5% in order to reign in credit supply.  This brought about an immediate US$300/t slide in copper cash quotes on the 14<sup>th</sup> to US$9326/t ($4.23/lb), and a further drop on the 18-19<sup>th</sup> when the ratio increase to 20.5% was indeed implemented.  Furthermore, news of record Chinese refined production during March – partly assisted by opportunities presented by halted output in Japan, threatened to take copper even lower on the 15<sup>th</sup> . But a subsequent data release indicating that Chinese warehouse stocks had fallen to a two-month low prompted a near US$100/t holding rally on cash copper, and countered fears of burgeoning stocks at a time of strong domestic refined production and imports. 

**Stocks fall on the SHFE…** At that time (April 15<sup>th</sup> ), warehouse stocks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange stood at 147.7kt, and represented the fourth consecutive weekly decline in recorded SHFE stocks – indeed, putting them at a level below that noted in mid-March, when two bonded warehouses (Tongshen Yangshan and Zhongchu Lin Gang), which had not been included before, formed part of the overall total figure as released by the Exchange and added 30.1kt.  SHFE data noted a week later on the 22<sup>nd</sup> then showed another fall of 8.6kt, to leave visible Chinese stocks at 139.1kt, the lowest level since early February and arguably the most bullish comment from China in several weeks. 

**..and the LME:SHFE differential gets interesting once again** That sharp price drop on the LME on April 13<sup>th</sup> was significant also for the relationship between copper prices in London and Shanghai.  For months there have been few opportunities for arbitrage deals between the two Exchanges.  But even though Shanghai copper prices had also been falling this month, the rate of their decline was slower than that seen on the LME.  On April 14<sup>th</sup> , the two price lines crossed over to leave Shanghai copper prices marginally ahead of the LME, and although we have not seen a consistent pattern just yet of higher Chinese quotes, the differential is now considerably narrower (+/- US$100/t) than it has been since last September.  Equally, there are some physical conditions in the Chinese market that are sufficiently encouraging to prompt t

he prospects of a more sustained interest by Chinese consumers in the red metal once again. 

**NBS semis and end-products data encouraging…** March data releases from China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) reveal some superficial contradictions which can only be explained by stock changes of intermediate copper semis.  National output of major electrical products, from trains to air conditioning sets, have all witnessed double digit growth during the first quarter _vs._ Q1 2010 (see the table below).  And yet a similar comparison of copper semis output shows a -1% contraction, from 224.4kt during Q1 2010 to 222.1kt during Q1 2011.

**..as it lends potential for stronger cathode buying in the near term** The weak semis production figures when set against the context of strong end-use output has to imply that de-stocking has been responsible for the apparent poor performance from the semis sector.  Note that we have calculated the percentage changes ourselves by comparing the year-on-year values for each category.  This is because there appear to be major discrepancies between the percentage changes quoted by the NBS for each category and the implied changes from a comparison of the underlying data.  As an example, the NBS quoted a year-on-year increase in Q1 copper semis output of 16.3% whereas a comparison of the actual data points to a decline of 1%.  Equally as worrying was the sudden uplift in reported semis production from the CNIA.  From a 2.1% cumulative decline in copper semis output year-on-year in January and February the CNIA Q1 2011 figure then leapt to a 14.5% increase over the same three month period in the prior year, implying an uplift of 51.5% in March’s output even though the actual data for March 2011 over March 2010 showed an increase of just 2.8%.  Focusing on actual data comparisons, the low growth in semis output has no doubt been aided by the tightening credit conditions, an unfavourable price arbitrage and high copper prices deterring new buying.  Furthermore, for the first two months of the year, the adjusted NBS (CNIA) data shows that semis output was -1.9% (-2.1%), and so the 3.5% (2.8%) improvement in March over the same month in 2010 should be viewed as a positive indicator of recent industrial activity. In ou

r view, then, provided that end-use output remains robust, at some point the pipeline between cathode consumers, semis manufacturers and end-users will need to be replenished, and this can only be good for cathode consumers given the compounding effect of re-stocking throughout the consumption chain. **For April, though, spot buying has been weak…** Although lower copper prices are once again drawing Chinese copper consumers back to new cathode rather than continuing with their previously high scrap usage, we have yet to see this pressure come to bear on spot premia. While our contacts have reported sporadic premia spikes to between RMB350-500/t from one day to the next, the average for the month has been RMB115-120/t, slightly lower than at the start of the month. Other regional premia show little change in most markets on last month, possibly with the exception of the USA, where tighter imports on tube products from countries proven last year to be dumping have encouraged domestic production and, hence, spurred demand for new cathode. **LME stocks rise, Comex dips slightly** Meanwhile, reasonably strong metal demand in Europe and the USA (see Consumption) have failed to halt the rise in LME stocks. Overall, LME stocks were up by over 22kt from the April opening tally of 437.9kt to 460.1kt on April 26th . Most of the increase has come at warehouses in South Korea. Comex stocks have remained relatively flat at 75.3kt on the 26th vs. 77kt on the 1st . **Few changes since last month’s report keeps tight metal outlook in place for this year** Only minor changes to our refined production and consumption estimates for this year have been required since our last report, trimming our projected deficit from 482kt to 412kt. The slight softening in April prices has prompted us to reduce our Q2 forecast average by 2% to US$9800/t ($4.45/lb). But the anticipated deficit for the remainder of the year and consequent tightening in metal stock days of consumption encourages us to retain our reasonably bullish outlook for the red metal. However, we are expecting better performances from the supply side as we move into 2012, and the c.400kt deficit projected for this year will largely be countered by an anticipated c.300kt surplus then. Even so, in terms of stock days, there will be little change in 2012, and so we continue to believe that there will be considerable pressure on prices to remain well above the four-dollar level for most of the year.

With global demand expectations now so closely wedded to the Chinese market given its relative size, it was always going to be its performance that determined the global outturn this year. However, after making her first tentative steps in March, Chinese consumption is beginning to ease down the aisle, with the groom, a market deficit, waiting gleefully at the altar. European demand has maintained its recent strength with producers reporting royally flush order books, while activity in North America has maintained a more cautious tone. However, the situation in Japan threatens to spoil the party, of late mostly because of the potential impact that prolonged disruptions to parts supply could have on global car production and the attendant impact on copper demand. ### **Europe and CIS** **Manufacturing continues to lead European economy** Euro zone industrial production expanded by 0.4% month on month and 7.3% year on year in February, as solid growth in Germany and Italy was offset by declining output in the periphery, mainly Ireland and Greece. The breakdown of data showed that production growth in capital and intermediate goods continued to outpace that of consumer durables and non-durables, highlighting that it is businesses not households in Europe that are driving the improvement. **ECB favours fight with inflation over growth** The preliminary Euro zone manufacturing PMI for April indicates that output will continue to expand in the coming

few months, but that growth could slow slightly.  The new orders index fell from 58.0 in March to 57.3 in April.  However, output faces headwinds from rising interest rates and the strength of the euro after the ECB raised interest rates from 1 to 1.25% in April, the first change in almost 2 years.  Further comments from ECB policy makers since then have increased market expectations of another rise within the next few months.  It seems that given a choice between keeping German inflation in check and aiding the recovery in the periphery, the ECB has ruled in favour of Germany. 

**Russian rod exports on the increase** Our discussions with market participants have pointed to most companies not noticing much Russian rod in Europe, despite our expectations of an increase after Russia re-imposed a duty on cathode exports.  However, latest trade data does in fact reveal a sharp increase in Russian exports of wire rod, up by 100% in the first two months of the year.  This ties in with our expectations but doesn’t explain why firms haven’t been feeling the increased competition.  Most of the material is heading into mainland Europe, with some also heading for Turkey. 

**Lightning rod market keeps up pace** We note that rod mills continue to report strong demand, with some surely picking up orders from Elektrokoppar and perhaps Russian exports have taken some of the business that they have withdrawn from.  One other explanation for European rod mills not noticing Russian material is that they are sufficiently happy with their own order intake because overall demand is so strong at the moment.  After all, it is generally in a weak market the producers start to worry about import competition. 

**High prices miniaturising growth elsewhere** Order activity in the rest of the semis market also remains robust, although there are at least some early signs of high copper prices tempering demand.  At this stage however, rather than causing a slide in consumption, lofty raw material costs are rather slowing the pace of growth.  Indeed, the topic of substitution has been on the tip of everyone’s lips for some time and losses in heat transfer applications are ongoing. The other trend that we have picked up on is miniaturisation of products.  Despite the fact that in making products smaller they often have to use costly high performance alloys to offset thinness, savings are still to be had from these design tweaks.  In summary, the appetite for orders remains firm for now, the above trends are eating into growth rates rather than taking a slice of the pie itself. 

**Construction market sees improvement** The construction market across Europe has struggled for some time now amid downbeat commercial and residential activity, and while there was some benefit from government spending previously, most of this has run out of steam amid “fiscal responsibility”.  However, Markit’s Eurozone Construction PMI has been above the 50 expansionary level for three months now, w

hile the German construction PMI revealed the fastest rate of output growth since the survey began in 1999.  Notably, German growth was driven by the commercial sector, pointing to firms becoming sufficiently confident in economic conditions to make capital investments.  This suggests that rod output will maintain current relatively high levels for the time being at least. 

**Germany provides the silver lining to cloudy transport market** Western European passenger vehicle registrations fell by 5% year on year in March, as solid growth in Germany and France was more than offset by a fall in registrations in Italy, Spain and the UK.  For Q1 as a whole, sales fell by 2.3% to 3.58m units. The UK’s SMMT highlighted that the decline in the UK was due to the weakness in retail sales, as opposed to fleet and business volumes, and was a result of the 2010 scrapping schemes having come to an end.  Further declines are expected in Q2.  However, Germany’s VDA reported that car exports increased by 11% year on year in the first quarter, while domestic registrations increased by 14%.  This has led to a 7.7% gain German car production in Q1 to 1.49m units.  However, the VDA was cautious about prospects for the road ahead, citing high oil prices and the Japan situation as major obstacles in the coming months.

Even so, the strength in German output remains positive for copper demand given the German cars are typically relatively copper-intensive. 

**Second half slowdown to temper full year growth** Despite the relatively upbeat assessment of current sectoral demand, we remain cautious on the second half of the year and we continue to expect relatively muted demand growth overall in 2011 of around 2%.  In particular, the auto market is a cause for concern given worries over the availability of component supplies in the near term. 

### **Americas** 

**Headline housing starts number improves in March…** Housing starts in the US bounced back in March by 7.2% month on month to an annual rate of 549,000 units.  Though this represents an improvement over February figures, when housing starts declined by 22% (the largest decline on record), the US housing sector remains exceptionally weak, weighed down by the overhang of vacant and foreclosed houses, tight mortgage conditions, and falling house prices. Housing starts in March remain 13.4% lower compared to a year ago, when the government tax incentives were still in place.  The National Association of Home Builders also reported this week that its housing market index, a measure of confidence in the sector, dropped in April. 

**..and the auto market steps up a gear during Q1** The US auto market had a solid first quarter.  Improving labour markets have been a boost to demand, helping sales in Q1 increase by 20.1% y-o-y.  The most recent data suggest smaller, fuel efficient vehicles have been particularly in demand due to

the rise in fuel prices, with the national average price per gallon now at the US$4 level.  Stronger demand has fed through into robust growth in production, with output in Q1 up by 15.2% y-o-y (and up by 19.4% in March alone).  However, the disruptions caused by the Japan earthquake and tsunami have only begun to be felt in April, with all of Toyota’s US plants cutting production by 70% between April 26 through to June 3.  Honda’s US and Canadian plants have slowed output since the end of March and will continue on a reduced schedule for perhaps a further month or two.  Nissan, meanwhile, closed its three US plants for six days this month and its two Mexican plants for five days.  Other plants have been forced to halt production due to a lack of spare parts, and as a result output growth will be slower during Q2.  At this point it is impossible to quantify the extent of disruption to US output in Q2, but JP Morgan has come up with a forecast drop of 52% y-o-y owing to a shortage of microcontrollers, of which the average car has 30-50. 

**First new copper rod line in decades** Last month we saw a potential new investment in the US copper tube sector from an offshore source (China’s Hunan Golden Dragon).  This month the wire rod sector learned it, too, will soon have a new name amongst its thinning ranks.  In what must be the first investment in a new copper wire rod plant in more than two decades on US soil, Fort Wayne, IN-based Steel Dynamics Inc and Spain’s La Farga Group will establish a new copper rod plant in Allen County, IN under the name SDI LaFarga LLC. 

Neither the exact location nor the size of the proposed US$39M investment have been decided, but the parent companies hope the new plant will be on line sometime during 2013.  Steel Dynamics, formed only in 1993, is better known for the rapid ascent to its current position of fifth largest US carbon steel products maker at 5.3M short tons.  But in October 2007 it bought its principal ferrous scrap supplier OmniSource Corp – also based in Fort Wayne, but drawing scrap from over 70 yards across the Midwest and southeast.  OmniSource was also the nation’s largest non-ferrous scrap metals processor, and currently ships much of its copper scrap to China. 

The LaFarga Group’s La Farga Lacambra subsidiary has used Properzi technology (55kt/a capacity) since 1986 to make copper rod and wire, billets and railway products using secondary copper materials; the La Farga Rod subsidiary makes electrolytic copper rod from HG cathodes from a newer (2008) 180kt/a capacity Properzi line; and the La Farga Tub subsidiary melts scrap copper to make plumbing, air-conditioning and refrigeration tube.  All production units are located on a single site near Barcelona.  The venture with Steel Dynamics is La Farga’s first foray outside Spain.  At this stage, we are assuming that the copper scrap that OmniSource currently exports to China will be retained for the SDI LaFarga plant, and that Properzi will provide

the technology.  If the latter proves correct, then we believe this will represent Properzi’s second rod line on US soil, following United Copper Industries’ 180kt/a capacity rod line installed in 1998. 

**Wire market under attack from copper-clad steel** Although the US copper rod market grew by almost 10% last year, to 1.262Mt, it has contracted each year for the prior eight years and remains just 60% of its past peak size in 1998.  By itself, then, the SDI LaFarga investment is bold indeed, but it is even more so in light of the constant discussion over substitution due to high copper prices.  This month we were also alerted to a contract won by Hickory, NC-based CommScope to supply two wind farm projects in Michigan and Iowa with its GroundSmart<sup>TM</sup> Copper-Clad Steel, an alternative to solid and stranded copper wire.  The product is an electrical conductor that has an outer sleeve of copper metallurgically bonded to a solid steel core.  The technology is not new, having been in use since the 1970s, but CommScope claims that the product is gaining credibility with utilities who are trying to reduce their investment costs and protect their new assets from theft.  Traditional copper wiring continues to be ripped out of any isolated installations by thieves for its value, but copper-clad steel would be incredibly difficult to re-process and easier to identify by source, and thus carries little recycling value at all.

### **China** 

**Economy yet to feel tightening pinch** Economic growth in China has shown little sign of slowing during the first quarter.  Real GDP expanded by 9.7% year on year in the first quarter compared with 9.8% in Q4, while industrial output grew by 13.3% year on year, compared with 13.5% in Q4.  Indeed, IP growth accelerated in March to 14.8% year on year, and fixed asset investment growth reached 25%.  As such, policy tightening in China has yet to have a noticeable impact and we don’t expect this to change significantly within the next few months. 

**Reserves and rates continue ascent** The Peoples Bank of China increased reserve requirements for banks to a record high last week, the tenth increase in the current tightening cycle.  This follows on from the fourth increase in interest rates in six months at the start of April.  These steps will not be the last tightening measures from the PBoC, as economic data suggests that the tightening carried out so far has had limited effect.  Indeed, the CPI measure of inflation accelerated to 5.4% in March, from 4.9% in February, taking inflation to its highest level since July 2008.  Credit expansion has slowed from the breakneck pace of 2009 and 2010, but the 16.6% year on year expansion in broad money supply in the first quarter was still relatively high. 

**Positive developments confirm our outlook** There have been some positive developments in the Chinese market over t

he course of the last month and not least that demand has continued to improve.  On the face of it, the 43% slump in imports of refined copper during Q1 paints a bleak picture for demand, which some felt needed to improve for the 2011 market to play out as expected.  However, the concentrate stock build in 2010, which we discussed last month, implies less of a need for refined copper imports this year and as such, the sluggish March number shouldn’t been mistaken for a harbinger of doom. 

**March semis output turns positive** Latest data from the CNIA does indeed point to Chinese semis output rising by 2.8% in March, following a flat year-on-year comparison in February and a decline the prior month.  Data have of course been somewhat distorted by the timing of the Chinese New Year in the first part of 2011 but for the quarter as a whole, output was broadly the same as last year. 

**Price dip triggers modest restock** Meanwhile, since around 11<sup>th</sup> April SHFE prices have generally been on a downward trajectory and softer prices have triggered a bit of opportunistic re-stocking at semis producers.  Overall inventories remain low, and hand-to-mouth cathode purchases remain a feature of the market, but the fact that there was modest re-stocking is suggestive of sufficient confidence in the demand outlook to warrant these purchases.  While SHFE prices were in decline, scrap prices held firm, which has resulted in tighter scrap spreads and made cathode a relatively more attractive option, which again is supporting refined copper purchases.  At the same time, SHFE stocks have been declining, again pointing to firm demand conditions. 

**Declining stocks underscore demand outlook** The other component of Chinese stocks that has been in focus has been those tied up in bonded warehouses.  As we have discussed this on these pages before, a significant proportion of these stocks are tied up in financing deals after having been imported on a letter of credit.  Chinese authorities have moved to clamp down on this and on the re-export of bonded material, which suggests that this material could quickly find its way into the domestic market.  This is important because one of the first signals for the second quarter upturn in demand that we are forecasting should be rising premia in Shanghai.  However, if a flood of bonded material were to hit the domestic market then this would depress premia even in the face of rising demand.  This then takes us back to relying on SHFE stock levels as a first indicator, which as we noted above, have been declining and thus pointing to the second quarter upturn that we have been forecasting. 

**AC output puts heat into tube production** Air conditioner production in the first 3 months of the year increased by 48.8% year on year, with the sharp increase driven by re-stocking at distributors and wholesalers ahead of the summer. In line with this, ACR tube production has maintained its pace into April, with most producer

s running at full capacity. However, some tube makers are cautious on the outlook given the high copper to aluminium price ratio, which has triggered substitution, in particular for connecting tube in air conditioners. Although this takes some of the shine off the longer term outlook, conditions remain firm for now. **Construction imbalance continues** Floor space under construction in the first quarter increased by 35% year on year, reflecting the massive amount of property in the pipeline (much of which is likely sitting idle). Needless to say, things have taken a severe downturn. The extent of the disruption to industry in Japan appears to be increasing rather than decreasing, as ripple effects spread through the supply chain. For example, 90% of global supply of BT resin (used to make circuit boards) is produced by two factories in Japan, both of which were damaged in the quake. The impact is greatest for Japanese industry as a whole vis-а-vis other countries, because the two industries most affected by supply disruptions are autos and electronics, which make up a large share of Japanese industry. On top of that, the common practice of just in time inventories in Japan has meant that producers have limited supplies to use up. **Full year implications for industrial output remain uncertain** At this point, it’s impossible to say how much IP will fall in Japan following the quake. At the end of March we changed our IP forecast for 2011 from +3.1% to -1.7%, but there’s a good chance that we are still too optimistic. One positive sign was that total exports in March fell by just 2.2% month on month, largely due to a 28% drop in vehicle exports (they account for ~10% of total shipments). This suggests that export infrastructure has held up reasonably well. **Disruptions continue at refineries and consumers** As we have discussed elsewhere in this report, operations at the Onahama refinery in Japan remain suspended but it is

n’t just smelters and refineries that are facing difficulties, with semis producers and firms even further downstream also enduring some disruptions.  Of note, Hitachi Cable’s plants in Ibaraki prefecture remain suspended at the time of writing, with lack of electricity, gas and water cited as being behind the closure. 

**Full year data reveal increased market share for transport** With 2010 now fully behind us, it is useful to take a look at the sectoral changes in copper demand over the course of the past year and also looking at trends further back.  The biggest and most obvious increase in sectoral share took place in the transportation sector, which increased from 9.7% in 2009 to 10.3% in 2010.  Admittedly, transportation’s share had dropped in 2009 from similar levels to today but looking further back, there is a clear trend in play of this sector gaining a larger slice of the copper pie.  What is even more impressive is that that absolute levels are increasing in addition to the percentage increase, compared to a declining market overall.  This trend is easily explained by the increase in electronic components and motors in vehicles, in addition to the expansion of electric and hybrid vehicles which are heavy users of copper.  Given expectations of green vehicles taking ever more share in future, we expect this trend of transport taking a larger share of the market to continue. 

**Electrical market steady as she goes** The largest end use market in Japan is electric and electronic products, which accounted for 39.1% of demand in 2010, up from 36.3% in 2009.  Over the past 15 years or so, the market has remained about the same size but this masks a decline in share to 2001 before a gradual recovery thereafter. 

**Construction loses share on sluggish building activity** Building and construction is the second largest sector but was the only one that actually declined in relative size last year, slipping from 33.0% share in 2009 to 28.9% last year. The Japanese construction market has been in the doldrums for several years now and a decline in the market share of this sector over the past few years is closely related to this. 

**Machinery and engineering ebbs lower** In the industrial machinery and engineering sector there has been a modest decline in market share over the past few years , although in 2010 its share increased to 6.7% from 6.5% the prior year. Finally, in the consumer and general products there seems to have been a gradual expansion on a five year period which culminated in market share of 15% in 2010, up from 14.5% in 2009.

**China’s Q1 2011 concentrate imports down by 16% on a year earlier** As mentioned, according to official customs statistics China’s imports of copper concentrates continue to underperform in relation to last year’s levels.  Receipts in March totalled 450.8kdmt which were 16.4% lower than in March 2010.  Likewise, cumulative imports of 1.42Mdmt were 16.6% below the tonnage recorded in the first three months of last year.  Chile’s contribution was down by 37% through March which translated into a market share of only 25%.  At the same time, Peruvian receipts also fell, by 17% and that country’s share of total imports was only 15.5%.  Mongolian deliveries were essentially flat on last year while marked increases were seen from Canada, Indonesia, Laos, Mauritania and Mexico. 

**Plenty of Chinese smelter projects – but will they be developed?** Chinese smelter projects continue to be announced on a regular basis with the latest coming from China Qinghai Baihe Aluminium who aims to have a 100kt/a greenfield copper smelter/refinery project constructed and placed into production by 2015.  According to the company it currently operates a copper mine in Qinghai that has a capacity to produce 50kt/a of metal in concentrates which would form the base feed for the smelter project.  However, upon closer scrutiny we find that China Qinghai Baihe Aluminium is a subsidiary of Western Mining and hence this project is actually the same as the one already announced by Western Mining.  Notwithstanding this, for the copper smelting industry outside of China, the sheer number and regularity with which these smelter projects crop up must be somewhat alarming.  However, it does appear that the Chinese authorities are now finally becoming far more serious about enforcing environmental legislation and energy efficiency which are viewed as key components of the country’s new 5 year plan.  As a consequence, Chinese companies wishing to build new copper smelting capacity are coming under far more scrutiny than has been the case in the past.  An Environmental Impact Assessm

ent (EIA) now has to be submitted and approved prior to any project being approved for construction. There are currently nine Chinese greenfield and brownfield smelter projects with a collective capacity of 1.1Mt/a Cu that have received EIA approval and that are under construction.  More significantly, there are at least twelve projects with a combined capacity of almost 2.5Mt/a Cu that have either had their EIAs turned down or that are awaiting EIA approval, with no guarantee that such approval will be forthcoming.  Another consequence of this hardened approach to smelting in the context of the environment has been the issuance of closure orders on all operations that are deemed to be using antiquated technology.  These plants should have been closed down several years ago under previously-introduced legislation; however, many survived in spite of this.  Now, however, all assets have come under closer scrutiny.  The main targets have been blast and reverberatory furnaces, although other technologies are also at risk.  Companies such as Chuxiong Yunxin, Huludao, Yunnan Tin and Zhongtiaoshan have already shut down their older units while Daye recently closed its reverberatory furnace and Noranda reactor in tandem with the commissioning of its new Ausmelt furnace.  All of these initiatives indicate to us that future growth in Chinese primary smelting capacity is likely to be pared back at a time when copper-in-concentrate mine production is growing strongly and assuming these initiatives are maintained, this should lead to a more balanced concentrate market within the next three years. 

**We have revised our Japanese smelter/refinery estimates for 2011** Most Japanese smelting companies have recently released their production intentions for the next six months (with the understandable exception of Mitsubishi Materials).  We have analysed this data and have revised our estimates for a number of these operations.  PPC restarted its Hitachi refinery during the third week of April and the company initially projected that the plant would produce 53.4kt of refined copper in the period April to September 2011 which represents a 42% year-on-year decline.  More recently, this forecast was raised by 7kt on the assumption that night time power can also be secured.  At the same time the company’s Saganoseki refinery is expected to produce 114.1kt which is up by 3.2kt on last year with its share from Tamano falling by 2.5% to 89.9kt. ## Production news 

**CESCO Week reveals various production problems at a number of Chilean copper operations** Mine disruptions were very much at the fore of conversations during CESCO Week.  Escondida is having its fair share with conveyor belt and SAG mill problems at its older concentrator.  In addition, Codelco’s Gaby mine has lost production on account of issues with its primary crusher.  Elsewhere, the Andacollo and Esperanza projects are both producing less copper than anticipated due to teething problems as they continue to ramp up output.  Heavy rains have also impacted the performances of both Collahuasi and Quebrada Blanca and we estimate that overall lost mine output in Chile has been almost 150kt Cu as a result of these issues. 

**Xstrata looks to maximise efficiencies at Ernest Henry by buying into Cloncurry** Xstrata has offered A$178M (US$185M) in cash to Exco Resources for the two areas of copper mineralization which comprise the Cloncurry Copper project in northwest Queensland.  The E1 Camp and the Monakoff group of deposits at Cloncurry have total resources of 55Mt containing 472kt Cu and almost 400kozs Au, with an open pit reserve of 28.1Mt assaying 0.83% Cu and 0.24g/t Au.  Exco was considering establishing a 25kt/a copper in concentrate mine at Cloncurry, starting from 2013.  Xstrata’s offer – if accepted by Exco shareholders – would bring Cloncurry’s ore to its Ernest Henry mill just 8km away to enhance the economics of both Cloncurry itself and the changeover now underway at EH.  This will see the conversion of Ernest Henry from a former 100kt/a+ open pit producer to a 50kt/a underground mine.  Consequently, there would be excess capacity at the mill which Cloncurry’s ores could partially fill.  Open pit mining at EH will come to an end in 2012, and the approval for the A$589M underground extension came at the end of 2009.

**Rosemont suffers another bureaucratic hiccup** The proposed Rosemont mine in Arizona has endured yet another bureaucratic setback from the US Forest Service regarding its issuance of a draft environmental impact statement (DEIS).  Most recently, Rosemont Copper was expecting to receive a copy of the DEIS last December, but the Service now says it will not be ready until January 2012.  This would represent almost three years of delay from the original Spring 2009 date that the Service had issued.  The Service cannot make a decision on Rosemont until it has compl

eted its own environmental assessment, and no mine construction can begin without this assessment.  Once the DEIS is released, the public has a 90-day period in which to lodge further complaints/objections, and given the project’s history, such complaints will likely be forthcoming.  Rosemont is located c.40km southeast of Tucson and has attracted intensive scrutiny from local opposition groups.  We have already pushed back any potential start at the mine from a 2013 date to late- 2014, but this latest delay could shunt start-up well into 2016.  Rosemont plans to be a 90kt/a copper in concentrate producer once at steady-state operations. 

**Thomson Creek secures major equipment for Mount Milligan** Thomson Creek Metals Co has passed one more milestone at its proposed Mount Milligan project in British Columbia by arranging US$132M worth of equipment financing with Cat Financial Services Ltd.  A full equipment fleet comprising haul trucks, shovels, drills, loaders and dozers will be delivered to the Mount Milligan site by the end of 2012, allowing the mine to start producing by late-2013.  We expect an average annual production of c.40kt/a copper in concentrate beginning 2014, and currently carry the project in our Highly Probable projects category. 

**BHPB progresses with Escondida expansion…** Late last month, BHP Billiton approved the Ore Access Project at its Escondida mine in Chile at a total cost of US$554M (US$319M by BHPB).  The project will re-locate the crushing and conveying facilities that are currently placed inside Escondida’s main open pit so that mining can access higher grade ore from 2013.  This should allow output of copper in concentrate to increase to 850-880kt during 2013-2014 from last year’s 787kt.  This year, lower ore grades, SAG mill and conveyor belt issues and this equipment relocation work will result in lower output (c.630kt copper in concentrate), but this should lift to 800kt in 2012. 

**..and also moves ahead at Olympic Dam** Virtually in the same breath of its news on Escondida, BHPB also noted that it had progressed expansion studies at its Olympic Dam operations to a feasibility study stage.  The company handed over its Supplementary Environmental Impact Statement (SEIS) to the Commonwealth Government (CG) last December, and is awaiting permission from the CG to publish the SEIS so that other government levels in South Australia and Northern Territory can assess the Olympic Dam expansion plans.  The plans call for a massive increase in output at the mine from the current levels of c.180kt/a to 750kt/a over the next 30 years.  We anticipate the first expansion stage (to 350kt/a) coming into view by H2 2017, with Stage II to 540kt/a being achievable within four years after that.  Output over the last couple of years has been pinned back to c.125-130kt/a levels following damage to the main haulage shaft, from the previous nine-year average of 185kt/a.

**Milpo wins Magistral – sets 2014 start date** Lima, Peru-based Cia Minera Milpo emerged as the winner of the bidding process to develop the Magistral copper-molybdenum property, formerly owned by Vancouver-based Inca Pacific Resources. **Grupo’s Q1 copper production and sales up by >13%** Higher output principally from the Buenavista complex in Sonora state, Mexico, offset lower production due to poorer grades elsewhere for Grupo Mexico during the first quarter. Mined copper output was up by 13.7% to 124.2kt, while refined production rose by nearly 15% to 129.2kt.  Sales also increased by 11.5% to 130.1%. **Rio Tinto looks to extend mine life at Bingham Canyon** Rio Tinto has granted its Kennecott Utah copper subsidiary US$238M in funds for a feasibility study designed to extend the mine life by nine years to 2028.
